title: Nuremberg trials
summary: From 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946, an International Military Tribunal set up by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union sat in Nuremberg's Palace of Justice. It tried 22 figures from Nazi Germany's diplomatic, economic, political and military leadership for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. It convicted 19, acquitted three and sentenced twelve to death. It established crimes against humanity as crimes under international law.

uncertainty.note: The tribunal opened on 20 November 1945 and delivered its verdict on 1 October 1946.

as_recorded.value: It formally opened in Nuremberg, Germany, on November 20, 1945, just six and a half months after Germany surrendered.
On October 1, 1946, the judges delivered their verdict.

In pursuance of the Agreement signed on the 8th day of August 1945 by the Government of the United States of America, the Provisional Government of the French Republic, the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, there shall be established an International Military Tribunal

where.modern_name: Nuremberg, Bavaria, Germany (city pin; the trial sat in the Palace of Justice)
where.historical_name: Palace of Justice, Nuremberg, Allied-occupied Germany

importance.justification: Held individuals responsible under international law and established crimes against humanity as international crimes.

audience_note: Addresses legal proceedings concerning the Holocaust, mass murder, slave labor, and Nazi atrocities.

reviewer_note: The US Holocaust Memorial Museum says 24 were indicted and 22 stood trial. It dates the verdict to 1 October 1946. The later Nuremberg proceedings are separate and not covered here.
